news_drafts.headline: Nottingham City sets aside £15.2m for schools-grant deficits, leaving general reserves at 8% of budget
news_drafts.lead:
Nottingham City Council has set aside £15.2m in its reserves against the chance that it cannot recover emerging deficits in the high needs part of the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The draft medium-term financial plan, before the Executive Board on 20 October 2026, puts its unallocated general fund reserves, the cushion for the unexpected, at £39.4m, or 8% of the 2027/28 budget.

That is below the 10% minimum recommended by the council's chief finance officer (the section 151 officer). The council began with £61.9m, 13% of the 2027/28 budget, and the forecast had fallen to £26.4m, 6%. After first-quarter budget monitoring and a pause in Local Government Reorganisation, £13m was moved from the council's reorganisation reserve into unallocated reserves, which brought the position to £39.4m. The paper calls the provision "prudent" and says the fall below the minimum is temporary.

The paper gives the reason for the provision as uncertainty over future national funding arrangements. The chief finance officer notes material uncertainty over the forecast DSG balance and over eligibility for 90% High Needs Stability Grant funding. The paper describes this as a national issue affecting authorities with unresolved DSG deficits. If the council receives DSG-related resilience funding, or the requirement falls, the provision would be released back into general fund reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire fire authority ended 2025/26 at £57.2m against a £57.4m budget, with a 2026/27 gap flagged
news_drafts.lead:
Nottinghamshire and City of Nottingham Fire and Rescue Authority spent £57.2m in 2025/26, against a revised budget of £57.4m, according to the draft annual report from its external auditor (the independent check on the council's accounts), which went to the authority's Finance and Resources Committee on 16 October.

The same report says the authority's medium-term financial strategy (its financial plan for the next few years, showing the gap between expected spending and expected income) identifies a possible funding shortfall for 2026/27. It attributes the gap to inflation pressures and uncertainty over funding allocations and pay awards. The report notes the strategy "also highlighted a funding shortfall that might necessitate utilising additional reserves for 2026/27". Reserves are money the authority has put aside.

The authority has built this into its reserve strategy, the report says, and holds enough reserves to cover the gap. The papers give no figure for the size of the shortfall or the amount of reserves that might be used.

news_drafts.headline: Nottingham City auditors expect to issue a disclaimer of opinion on accounts by 30 November 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Grant Thornton, Nottingham City Council's external auditor, expects to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the council's accounts by 30 November 2026, according to its progress report to the Audit Committee. A disclaimer means the auditors cannot say whether the financial statements are fairly presented. The report says the date follows the committee's meeting on 27 November 2026.

The disclaimer follows a multi-year "Regaining Assurance" programme begun after the council breached the ringfence around its housing revenue account (the separate account for its own housing stock, paid for by rents). The council delivered its draft accounts on time. The auditors say their risk assessment still factors in "historic weaknesses in the control environment" identified by independent reviews after the breach. Internal audit has done limited work on journal controls, authorisation limits and segregation of duties in 2024/25 and 2025/26. Payroll testing found three leavers for whom supporting documents were missing.

The auditors say the finance team focused on meeting the 30 June statutory deadline for publishing draft accounts and did not provide information to the agreed timetable, so interim testing was delayed. Fifteen information requests were outstanding on 15 September. Against a 100% target, 25% of papers were delivered by 5 June, 43% by 15 June and 32% by 30 June.

Two further queries are open. One concerns the nature of the council's LOBO loans (bank loans where the lender may propose a higher rate on set dates and the council may repay instead of accepting it), which the auditors say may complicate work on financial instruments. The other concerns the information behind the group audit strategy. An assessment of whether group organisations account under different frameworks has been requested but not provided, and is rated red for the 30 November deadline.

The auditors say the audit is further advanced than at the same point last year. A Regaining Assurance Strategy report went to the committee in June, and an assessment of the timeline for rebuilding assurance was sent to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the audit appointments body PSAA at the end of July.

findings.paper_title: MTFP272806 EIA - Additional Hours for Library Service Provision - Final signed 05.10.2026
findings.headline: Library service hours to be partially restored following 12-month review that measured 27% decline in visits and significant accessibility impacts from 2025 cuts
findings.detail: Library opening hours were reduced by 205.5 hours per week from August 2025 to achieve budget savings. A 12-month review measured: 27% reduction in library visits, 20% reduction in book issues, 12% reduction in computer usage, and 34% reduction in Saturday visits at some locations. The council proposes restoring 66.5 hours per week to address reduced accessibility for working people and families, operational challenges in Joint Service Centres, and customer dissatisfaction. The decision is due in October 2026.
findings.matters: Shows whether service-level austerity measures achieve expected savings and remain sustainable; demonstrates whether significant usage declines force councils to reverse or modify planned cuts
findings.figures: 205.5 hours per week cut from August 2025; 66.5 hours per week proposed restoration; 27% reduction in library visits; 20% reduction in book issues; 12% reduction in computer usage; 34% reduction in Saturday visits at Joint Service Centres and community libraries
findings.quote: The findings demonstrate that, whilst the reduced opening hours contributed towards the required savings, they have also had a significant impact on service usage and accessibility in a number of locations and at particular times.

findings.headline: Capital programme anticipated to generate revenue savings from reduced reactive repairs, but quantum of savings has not been calculated
findings.detail: The report states that capital works are anticipated to have positive impact on revenue spend through savings from reactive and on-going repairs. However, it explicitly notes that the total value of this saving has not yet been quantified. The council has not validated what reduction in reactive maintenance spend will actually be achieved.
findings.matters: Finance officers evaluate whether capital investment delivers operational cost reduction that offsets capital cost. Unquantified benefits weaken accountability; anticipated savings that are not measured often do not materialise. This affects the true financial cost of the programme.
findings.figures: No figures provided for anticipated savings
findings.quote: It is anticipated that these capital works will have a positive impact on revenue spend, for example, savings related to reactive and on-going repairs. The total value of this saving has not yet been quantified.

findings.headline: Construction market volatility creates identified risk that approved budget will be insufficient, with potential requirement to draw reserves or reduce scope
findings.detail: The paper states escalating costs may reduce scope deliverable within the approved £19m envelope. It cites UK construction industry downturn, labour shortages, and material cost inflation. It explicitly warns that geopolitical tensions have created capital funding risks from inflationary pressure resulting in overspend against budgets, and that for Nottingham City this may necessitate increased capital need, reserve drawdown or further project descoping.
findings.matters: Finance directors assess budget adequacy and contingency. The council's explicit identification that costs may exceed budget and force either reserve drawdown or further scope cuts is a material financial risk signal and a shared pressure across councils procuring construction work.
findings.figures: Approved budget £19,001,300; escalation risk amount not quantified
findings.quote: What this may mean for NCC is an increased need for capital, the use of reserves and potentially project descoping.

findings.headline: Council approves £19,001,300 three-year capital programme for health and safety works, funded from capital receipts, against £30,038,238 of identified works
findings.detail: A condition survey identified £30,038,238 of priority works across the operational estate. The council approves £19,001,300 over three years to address the highest priority element, deferring approximately £11m. Funding will come from capital receipts; the paper states there is no external funding available. This means drawing down reserves rather than borrowing.
findings.matters: The funding source choice (receipts rather than borrowing) signals reserve position and debt capacity. The gap between identified need and approved spend indicates either resource constraint or prioritisation of only the most urgent works.
findings.figures: £19,001,300 approved; £30,038,238 total identified works; three-year programme
findings.quote: Due to the urgency of the works, it is recommended that these capital projects are funded by capital receipts as there is no external funding available.

findings.headline: £15.2m provision created against non-recovery of emerging Dedicated Schools Grant high needs deficits amid national funding uncertainty
findings.detail: Council has made prudent provision of £15.2m in reserves against potential non-recovery of emerging Dedicated Schools Grant pressures in high needs block. Section 151 Officer notes this reflects material uncertainty as to forecast on DSG balance and eligibility for 90% High Needs Stability Grant funding. This is national issue affecting authorities across system with unresolved DSG deficits. If council receives DSG-related resilience funding or requirement reduces, provision would be released back to General Fund reserves.
findings.matters: Signals underlying special educational needs and high needs demand pressure potentially unfunded at national level; provision of this scale indicates material contingency against demand-led exposure; reflects systemic national funding issue.
findings.figures: DSG high needs provision £15.2m; if released, would restore unallocated reserves toward Section 151 Officer 10% minimum
findings.quote: The forecast reserve position indicates that unallocated General Fund reserves will temporarily reduce below the minimum level recommended by the Section 151 Officer. This reduction is primarily due to the creation of a prudent provision of approximately £15.2m against the potential non-recovery of emerging Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) pressures, reflecting uncertainty around future national funding arrangements

editorial.headline: Nottingham City audit opinion disclaimed as joint venture reserves depleted
editorial.standfirst: Depleted reserves in a 50:50 partnership and governance weaknesses have left the council without financial buffer or clean audit bill.
editorial.body:
Nottingham City Council faces a compounding set of financial and governance pressures that have left it without the reserves to absorb further shocks.

The council is a 50:50 partner in East Midlands Shared Services. As of 31 March 2026, EMSS reserves were fully depleted. The council's papers presented to June's joint committee meeting state: "The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis." This leaves Nottingham City liable for half of any cost overrun.

A month later, Grant Thornton, the council's external auditor, issued a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts—a rare step indicating it cannot form a view on the reliability of the financial statements. The council's papers presented to July's corporate scrutiny committee describe the work underway: "Council works closely with the External Auditor to identify the key information and evidential requirements that the auditor will need to provide a positive non-qualified audit opinion from a standard base disclaimed opinion."

But internal audit tells a deeper story. As of 31 July, the Head of Internal Audit's annual opinion for 2025/26 provides only Moderate Assurance. The audit committee papers state: "Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas." Multiple service areas remain problematic. The papers identify Adult Social Care performance and statutory compliance as an ongoing governance issue. Children's Services and Housing Services require continued improvement. Workforce capacity and resilience are constrained.

Compounding these issues is a pay award pressure. The council budgeted 3.5%, but the employers' current offer stands at 3.2%. The EMSS papers note: "Early indications suggest this offer will be rejected, with negotiations ongoing. Consequently, there remains a risk that the final award may be higher than the provision made in the budget for 2026/27."

The combination—zero reserves, audit failure, governance weaknesses not yet embedded—leaves little room for manoeuvre if budget pressures intensify.
editorial.pull_quote: Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas
editorial.watch_next: Grant Thornton is targeting a non-qualified audit opinion by March 2028, when the council's remediation efforts must demonstrate concrete results.
